Yes. Under the stated non-induced-star and partial-colouring definitions, all the proposed formulas and equality classifications are correct. The two delicate parts—the witness count for minimal forming sets and the equality analysis for five colours—both admit complete structural proofs.For every finite  $n$ -vertex graph  $H$ ,
$$\boxed{SF_2(P(H))=\Omega(P(H))=n+\delta(H)=2n-\nu(D(H)).}$$
Moreover,
$$\boxed{
\max_{|V(H)|=n}\bigl(SF_2(P(H))-\beta_2(P(H))\bigr)
=\max(0,n-4).
}$$
For  $n\ge5$ , the equality bases are exactly the graphs obtained from  $K_n$  by deleting a matching.For those bases, the four values are:Base  $H=K_n-mK_2$ ,  $n\ge5$  $\beta_2(P(H))$  $\psi_\square(P(H))$  $SF_2(P(H))$  $\Omega(P(H))$  $m=0,1$  $4$  $4$  $n$  $n$  $2\le m\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$  $4$  $5$  $n$  $n$ Here are proofs, including the small-size cases and the scope of the general paired-graph argument.1. Preliminary factsWrite  $N_S(x)=N_G(x)\cap S$ . An outside vertex  $x\notin S$  is formed precisely when
$$|N_S(x)|\ge2,$$
or  $x$  has a neighbour  $y\in S$  with  $N_S(y)\ne\varnothing$ . This uses non-induced copies of  $K_{1,2}$ ; an additional edge among the three vertices causes no problem.The forming property is upward closed: enlarging  $S$  preserves every required star for vertices that remain outside. Consequently, checking that every single-vertex deletion fails is sufficient for inclusion-minimality.Your partial-colouring condition is the sub-quorum condition: uncoloured vertices are omitted from the closed-neighbourhood count. arxiv.org All the arguments below use that precise condition.A useful general inequalityIn addition to the stipulated
$$\beta_2(G)\le\psi_\square(G)\le\Omega(G),$$
we have
$$\boxed{\beta_2(G)\le SF_2(G)}
\tag{1}$$
for every finite graph.Indeed, let  $A$  be a maximum dissociation set. For every  $x\notin A$ , the graph  $G[A\cup\{x\}]$  contains a  $K_{1,2}$ , since otherwise  $A\cup\{x\}$  would be a larger dissociation set. Every such star contains  $x$ , because  $G[A]$  contains none. Thus  $A$  is forming.After deleting any  $a\in A$ , the newly outside vertex  $a$  cannot be formed: the relevant graph is  $G[A]$ , which contains no  $K_{1,2}$ . Hence  $A$  is inclusion-minimal forming, proving (1).The deficiency identityThe stated identity
$$\delta(H)=n-\nu(D(H))
\tag{2}$$
is also correct for arbitrary  $H$ .The defect form of Hall’s theorem gives
$$n-\nu(D(H))
=\max_{A\subseteq V(H)}\bigl(|A|-|N_H(A)|\bigr).$$
Here, for a non-independent  $A$ , the neighbourhood  $N_H(A)$  may meet  $A$ .Set
$$I_A=A\setminus N_H(A).$$
Then  $I_A$  is independent and
$$N_H(I_A)\subseteq N_H(A)\setminus A.$$
Therefore
$$\begin{aligned}
|A|-|N_H(A)|
&=|A\setminus N_H(A)|-|N_H(A)\setminus A|\\
&\le |I_A|-|N_H(I_A)|.
\end{aligned}$$
Thus maximizing over all subsets gives the same answer as maximizing over independent sets, establishing (2).2. The general paired-graph theoremLet  $G$  have  $2n$  vertices and a fixed-point-free involutory automorphism  $\tau$ , with
$$v\sim\tau(v)\qquad\text{for every }v.$$
Call the two-element orbits rungs. Let  $H$  be the simple quotient whose vertices are the rungs, with two distinct quotient vertices adjacent whenever any edge joins their rungs.One observation will be used repeatedly:If two rungs are adjacent in the quotient, each endpoint of either rung has a neighbour in the other rung.This follows by applying  $\tau$  to any edge between them. It holds for parallel edges, cross edges, and the presence of both.We prove
$$\boxed{\Omega(G)=n+\delta(H),\qquad SF_2(G)\le n+\delta(H).}
\tag{3}$$
2.1 Exact evaluation of  $\Omega(G)$ Take a feasible pair  $(T,M)$ , and write
$$P=V(M),\qquad Z=V(G)\setminus(T\cup P).$$
Each rung has one of the six types
$$TT,\ ZZ,\ TP,\ PZ,\ TZ,\ PP.$$
Let  $a,b,u,v$  count the first four types, respectively. Since
$$|M|=\frac{|P|}{2},$$
summing the contribution of each rung gives
$$|T|+|M|=n+a-b+\frac{u-v}{2}.
\tag{4}$$
The injection  $TP\to PZ$ . Consider a  $TP$  rung  $\{t,p\}$ , where  $t\in T$ ,  $p\in P$ , and  $p=\tau(t)$ . Let  $q$  be the actual matching mate of  $p$ .Because  $t$  already has the selected neighbour  $p$ , feasibility forces  $t$  to have no other neighbour in  $T\cup P$ . Applying  $\tau$  to the matching edge  $pq$  gives
$$t\sim\tau(q).$$
Moreover,  $\tau(q)\ne p$ , since  $q\ne t$  and  $T\cap P=\varnothing$ . Hence  $\tau(q)\in Z$ , whereas  $q\in P$ . The rung of  $q$  has type  $PZ$ .This assignment is injective: a  $PZ$  rung has a unique  $P$ -endpoint, and that endpoint has a unique matching mate. Thus
$$u\le v.
\tag{5}$$
Let  $I$  be the quotient vertices corresponding to  $TT$  rungs. Each endpoint of a  $TT$  rung already has its unique permitted selected neighbour, its rung mate. Consequently: $I$  is independent in  $H$ ;every rung in  $N_H(I)$  has type  $ZZ$ .In particular,  $b\ge |N_H(I)|$ . Equations (4) and (5) yield
$$|T|+|M|
\le n+a-b
\le n+|I|-|N_H(I)|
\le n+\delta(H).$$
For attainment, choose an independent set  $I$  attaining  $\delta(H)$ , and put
$$J=N_H(I),\qquad R=V(H)\setminus(I\cup J).$$
Take both endpoints of every  $I$ -rung as  $T$ , and take the rungs over  $R$  as  $M$ . Every vertex of  $T$  has exactly one neighbour in  $T\cup V(M)$ , its rung mate. Therefore this is feasible, with value
$$2|I|+|R|
=n+|I|-|J|
=n+\delta(H).$$
This proves the  $\Omega$  equality in (3).2.2 The upper bound for  $SF_2(G)$ Let  $S$  be an inclusion-minimal forming set. Partition its doubly selected rungs into: $\mathcal C_0$ : rungs whose selected edge is an isolated component of  $G[S]$ ; $\mathcal C_1$ : all other doubly selected rungs.Let  $\mathcal Z$  be the empty rungs.We count witnesses only for deletions of endpoints of  $\mathcal C_1$ -rungs.Every such deletion has an original outside witnessFix an endpoint  $s$  of a rung in  $\mathcal C_1$ . At least one of  $s,\tau(s)$  has a selected neighbour outside their rung.If  $s$  has such a neighbour, then after deleting  $s$ , the newly outside vertex  $s$  has at least two selected neighbours. Otherwise  $\tau(s)$  has such a neighbour and remains active after the deletion. In either case,  $s$  itself is formed by  $S\setminus\{s\}$ .Minimality therefore supplies some original outside vertex  $x\notin S$  that fails to form after deleting  $s$ .Such a witness lies on an empty rungSuppose instead that  $y=\tau(x)\in S$ . Since  $s$  lies on a doubly selected rung,  $y\ne s$ , so  $y$  remains selected. Failure at  $x$  forces
$$N_{S\setminus\{s\}}(x)=\{y\},
\qquad
N_{S\setminus\{s\}}(y)=\varnothing.
\tag{6}$$
If  $x\sim s$ , applying  $\tau$  gives
$$y\sim\tau(s),$$
contradicting the second condition in (6).If  $x\not\sim s$ , then  $N_S(x)=\{y\}$ . Since  $x$  originally formed,  $y$  originally had a selected neighbour. The second condition in (6) forces this neighbour to be  $s$ . Applying  $\tau$  to  $y\sim s$  gives
$$x\sim\tau(s),$$
contradicting the first condition in (6).Thus  $\tau(x)\notin S$ , and the witness rung is empty.An empty rung witnesses at most two relevant deletionsFor an empty rung  $z$ , define
$$W_z=
\left\{
s:\begin{array}{l}
s\text{ is an endpoint of a }\mathcal C_1\text{-rung, and}\\
\text{some endpoint of }z\text{ fails after deleting }s
\end{array}
\right\}.$$
First suppose  $z$  is adjacent in  $H$  to a doubly selected rung  $c$ . Each endpoint of  $z$  has a forming star using the two endpoints of  $c$ : take a neighbour in  $c$ , followed by the selected rung edge. These stars survive every deletion outside  $c$ . Hence
$$W_z\subseteq V(c),\qquad |W_z|\le2.
\tag{7}$$
If  $c\in\mathcal C_0$ , its endpoints are excluded from the deletions counted by  $W_z$ , so
$$W_z=\varnothing.
\tag{8}$$
Now suppose  $z$  has no doubly selected neighbour. Fix one endpoint  $x$  of  $z$ . It is not adjacent to any relevant deletion vertex  $s$ , so deleting  $s$  does not change  $N_S(x)$ .If the deletion makes  $x$  fail, necessarily
$$N_S(x)=\{y\},\qquad N_S(y)=\{s\}.
\tag{9}$$
Indeed, two selected neighbours of  $x$  would survive, while zero selected neighbours would contradict original formation. With exactly one, failure means that this neighbour becomes isolated.The fixed vertex  $y$  has a unique selected neighbour  $s$ . Thus  $x$  witnesses at most one relevant deletion. Applying this to both endpoints proves  $|W_z|\le2$  also in this case.Completing the countThe quotient set  $\mathcal C_0$  is independent, and
$$N_H(\mathcal C_0)\subseteq\mathcal Z.
\tag{10}$$
Otherwise an isolated selected rung edge would have an additional selected neighbour.Every one of the  $2|\mathcal C_1|$  relevant endpoints has an empty-rung witness. Equations (7)–(10) therefore imply
$$2|\mathcal C_1|
\le \sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}|W_z|
\le 2\bigl(|\mathcal Z|-|N_H(\mathcal C_0)|\bigr).
\tag{11}$$
Finally,
$$|S|=n+|\mathcal C_0|+|\mathcal C_1|-|\mathcal Z|,$$
and hence
$$|S|
\le n+|\mathcal C_0|-|N_H(\mathcal C_0)|
\le n+\delta(H).$$
This proves (3).The scope here matters: for general paired graphs, the  $SF_2$  statement is an upper bound. For example,  $K_6$  with any three-rung pairing has quotient  $K_3$ , so  $\Omega(K_6)=3$ , whereas  $SF_2(K_6)=2$ . Prism attainment requires the additional construction below.3. Prism attainment for every base graphLet  $I$  be any independent set attaining  $\delta(H)$ , and write
$$J=N_H(I),\qquad R=V(H)\setminus(I\cup J).$$
The residual graph has no isolated vertexSuppose  $r\in R$  were isolated in  $H[R]$ . By the definition of  $R$ , it also has no neighbour in  $I$ . Thus
$$N_H(r)\subseteq J.$$
The independent set  $I\cup\{r\}$  would have the same neighbourhood  $J$  as  $I$ , increasing deficiency by one. This contradicts criticality.Therefore
$$H[R]\text{ has no isolated vertex}.
\tag{12}$$
In particular,  $|R|=1$  cannot occur for a critical  $I$ ; the proposed separate bound for that hypothetical case is harmless.Label prism vertices  $v_0,v_1$ , and define
$$S=\{i_0,i_1:i\in I\}\cup\{r_0:r\in R\}.
\tag{13}$$
This set is forming:For  $j\in J$ , choose  $i\in I\cap N_H(j)$ . Each  $j_\ell$  lies in the star  $j_\ell-i_\ell-i_{1-\ell}$ .For  $r\in R$ , choose  $q\in R\cap N_H(r)$ , using (12). The outside vertex  $r_1$  lies in the star  $r_1-r_0-q_0$ .It is inclusion-minimal:Deleting  $r_0$  leaves the original outside vertex  $r_1$  with no selected neighbour. The only selected bottom vertices have indices in  $I$ , and there are no edges from  $R$  to  $I$ .Deleting  $i_\ell$  leaves the newly outside vertex  $i_\ell$  with exactly one selected neighbour,  $i_{1-\ell}$ , which is isolated. Here  $I$  is independent and has no edges to  $R$ .Thus
$$SF_2(P(H))\ge |S|
=2|I|+|R|
=n+\delta(H).$$
Combining with the paired-graph upper bound proves
$$\boxed{SF_2(P(H))=\Omega(P(H))=n+\delta(H).}
\tag{14}$$
The constructed set need not be dissociation: its selected top vertices induce  $H[R]$ .4. The sharp dissociation gap and all equality basesLet  $r=|R|$ , retaining the critical-set decomposition above. There are no edges between the  $I$ -rungs and the prism over  $H[R]$ , so
$$\beta_2(P(H))
\ge 2|I|+\beta_2(P(H[R])).
\tag{15}$$
For every graph  $F$  on  $r$  vertices,
$$\beta_2(P(F))\ge\min(r,4).
\tag{16}$$
Explicit choices establish this directly:For  $r\le2$ , select  $r$  top vertices.For  $r=3$ , select two top vertices and the bottom vertex of the unused index.For  $r\ge4$ , select two top vertices and two bottom vertices, using four distinct indices.Each layer contributes at most two selected vertices, and there are no selected rungs in the latter two constructions. Therefore every selected vertex has degree at most one.Using (14)–(16),
$$\begin{aligned}
SF_2(P(H))-\beta_2(P(H))
&\le (2|I|+r)-(2|I|+\min(r,4))\\
&=\max(0,r-4)\\
&\le\max(0,n-4).
\end{aligned}
\tag{17}$$
For  $n\le4$ , inequality (1) supplies the reverse bound zero, so the gap is zero for every base graph. For  $n\ge5$ ,  $K_n$  attains  $n-4$ , as also follows from the characterization below.Positive equality forces  $\delta(H)=0$  and  $\beta_2(P(H))=4$ Suppose  $n\ge5$  and the gap is  $n-4$ . Equation (17) forces
$$\max(0,r-4)=n-4>0,$$
so  $r=n$ . Thus  $I=J=\varnothing$ , and
$$\delta(H)=0,\qquad SF_2(P(H))=n,\qquad\beta_2(P(H))=4.
\tag{18}$$
Characterizing dissociation number fourFor  $n\ge5$ ,
$$\boxed{\beta_2(P(H))=4\iff \Delta(\overline H)\le1.}
\tag{19}$$
For necessity, suppose a vertex  $v$  has distinct nonneighbours  $a,b$ . The top triple
$$\{v_0,a_0,b_0\}$$
induces at most the single edge  $a_0b_0$ , so it is dissociation. Choose two further indices  $c,d$ , possible because  $n\ge5$ , and add  $c_1,d_1$ . The bottom pair induces at most one edge, and no selected rung joins the layers. This gives a dissociation set of size five.For sufficiency, suppose the missing edges of  $H$  form a matching. Every three vertices of  $H$  induce either  $K_3$  or  $P_3$ , since at most one of their three possible edges can be missing. Hence a dissociation set in the prism contains at most two vertices in each layer. Its size is at most four, and four are attained using two vertices per layer with four distinct indices.Finally, these bases have  $\delta(H)=0$ . Every independent set has size at most two. For a singleton,
$$1-\deg_H(v)\le3-n<0.$$
An independent pair is a missing edge, and its neighbourhood consists of all other  $n-2$  vertices, giving deficiency
$$2-(n-2)=4-n<0.$$
Thus the empty set attains the maximum deficiency zero.This proves both the extremal value and the complete positive equality classification.5. Exact sub-quorum values for near-complete prismsNow let
$$H=K_n-mK_2,\qquad n\ge5.$$
We already know
$$\beta_2(P(H))=4,\qquad SF_2(P(H))=\Omega(P(H))=n.$$
It remains to prove the proposed values of  $\psi_\square$ .5.1 The exact local inequalityConsider either layer of a valid partial colouring. Let  $a$  be its number of coloured vertices. For a coloured vertex  $v$ , let  $r$  be the number of occurrences of its colour in that layer.Define four indicators: $\varepsilon=1$  if its possible same-layer nonneighbour is coloured; $\eta=1$  if that nonneighbour has  $v$ 's colour; $t=1$  if its rung partner is coloured; $s=1$  if its rung partner has  $v$ 's colour.The coloured closed neighbourhood has size  $a-\varepsilon+t$ , with  $r-\eta+s$  occurrences of  $v$ 's colour. The quorum condition is exactly
$$2r\ge a-\varepsilon+2\eta+t-2s.
\tag{20}$$
Consequently,
$$2r\ge a-2,
\tag{21}$$
and, when  $s=0$ ,
$$2r\ge a-1.
\tag{22}$$
One stronger special case will determine equality. If  $a=3$ ,  $r=1$ , and  $s=0$ , then  $\eta=0$ , and (20) forces
$$\boxed{\varepsilon=1,\qquad t=0.}
\tag{23}$$
Such a vertex must have its missing-edge mate coloured in the same layer, and its rung partner must be uncoloured.5.2 Classification of layers with at least three coloursSuppose the layer uses  $q\ge3$  colours. Equation (21) implies that every colour multiplicity is at least
$$\left\lceil\frac{a-2}{2}\right\rceil.$$
Summing multiplicities shows that the only possibilities are
$$(a,q)=(3,3),(4,3),(4,4),(6,3).$$
Their necessary cross-layer sharing is: $(a,q)$ Colour multiplicitiesColours necessarily appearing in the other layer $(3,3)$  $1,1,1$ At least  $1$  $(4,3)$  $2,1,1$ At least  $2$  $(4,4)$  $1,1,1,1$ All  $4$  $(6,3)$  $2,2,2$ All  $3$ For  $(3,3)$ , at least one vertex of the triple has no missing-edge mate inside it, since the missing edges form a matching. By (23), that vertex must have a rung partner of its own colour.For  $(4,3)$ , each singleton colour violates (22) unless its vertex has a same-coloured rung partner. The same reasoning applies to every vertex in the  $(4,4)$  case.For  $(6,3)$ , every colour has multiplicity two, and
$$2r=4<5=a-1.$$
Thus every vertex has a same-coloured rung partner.Every other layer has at most two colours.5.3 At most five colours, with rigid equalityLet  $q_0,q_1$  be the layer colour counts and  $h$  the number of colours shared between layers. The total is
$$q_0+q_1-h.$$
If both layer counts are at most two, this is at most four. If one layer has four colours, all four are shared, and the total is again at most four.In the remaining cases each layer has at most three colours. A three-colour layer shares at least one colour, so:one three-colour layer and one layer with at most two colours give at most four;two three-colour layers give at most five.Hence
$$\psi_\square(P(H))\le5.
\tag{24}$$
Equality five requires
$$q_0=q_1=3,\qquad h=1.
\tag{25}$$
The table then forces exactly three coloured vertices in each layer, each with a different colour: a four-vertex three-colour layer would force at least two shared colours, and a six-vertex layer would force three.Let  $\alpha$  be the unique shared colour. In either layer, the two vertices of nonshared colours satisfy (23). Both must have their missing-edge mates inside the triple. Since missing edges form a matching, these two vertices must be each other’s missing-edge mates.The remaining vertex—the  $\alpha$ -vertex—has no missing-edge mate inside the triple, so it must have a same-coloured rung partner. Thus the two  $\alpha$ -vertices are rung mates.Equation (23) also says that every nonshared-colour leaf has an uncoloured rung partner. Therefore the missing pair used in the top layer and the missing pair used in the bottom layer are distinct. In particular,
$$\psi_\square(P(H))=5\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m\ge2.
\tag{26}$$
This proves a full support characterization: every five-colour colouring consists of exactly one full central rung, one top missing pair, and a different bottom missing pair, with one shared central colour and four distinct leaf colours.5.4 AttainmentIf  $m\ge2$ , choose two missing pairs  $\{a,b\}$ ,  $\{d,e\}$ , and an index  $c$  outside their four endpoints. Such  $c$  exists because  $n\ge5$ .Colour  $c_0,c_1$  with  $\alpha$ , and colour
$$a_0,\ b_0,\ d_1,\ e_1$$
with four distinct new colours. Leave all other vertices uncoloured.Each central vertex has a coloured closed neighbourhood of size four, containing two vertices of colour  $\alpha$ . Each leaf has a coloured closed neighbourhood consisting of itself and its centre. Every quorum condition therefore holds, with five colours.Four colours are always attainable by giving distinct colours to the four vertices of a dissociation set. Combining this with (24)–(26) proves
$$\boxed{
\psi_\square(P(K_n-mK_2))
=
\begin{cases}
4,&m\le1,\\
5,&m\ge2.
\end{cases}}
\tag{27}$$
6. Small sizes, structural consequences, and a sharper gap theoremAll four parameters coincide for  $n\le4$ From (1), (14), and (17),
$$\beta_2(P(H))=SF_2(P(H))=\Omega(P(H))
\qquad(n\le4).$$
The stipulated sandwich for  $\psi_\square$  gives
$$\boxed{
\beta_2(P(H))
=\psi_\square(P(H))
=SF_2(P(H))
=\Omega(P(H))
=n+\delta(H)
\quad(n\le4).
}
\tag{28}$$
This includes  $n=0$  under the usual empty-graph convention.The complete-base structural assertions holdFor  $n\ge5$ ,  $P(K_n)$  is  $n$ -regular. Simultaneous permutations of the indices, together with layer interchange, act transitively on its vertices.Deleting fewer than  $n$  vertices leaves a nonempty clique in each layer and at least one intact rung, because the  $n$  rungs are vertex-disjoint. Thus the surviving graph is connected. Deleting all  $n$  neighbours of one vertex isolates it while leaving other vertices, proving
$$\kappa(P(K_n))=n.$$
Consequently,
$$\beta_2(P(K_n))=\psi_\square(P(K_n))=4,
\qquad SF_2(P(K_n))=\Omega(P(K_n))=n,$$
giving the claimed unbounded gaps within this regular, highly connected, vertex-transitive family.A sharp companion theorem for the colouring gapThe package also yields
$$\boxed{
\max_{|V(H)|=n}
\bigl(SF_2(P(H))-\psi_\square(P(H))\bigr)
=\max(0,n-4).
}
\tag{29}$$
Indeed,
$$SF_2-\psi_\square
\le SF_2-\beta_2
\le\max(0,n-4),$$
and  $K_n$  attains the bound for  $n\ge5$ .For  $n\ge5$ , equality in (29) forces equality in the dissociation-gap theorem, hence  $H=K_n-mK_2$ , and also forces  $\psi_\square=\beta_2=4$ . Equation (27) then gives  $m\le1$ . Therefore the positive equality bases for the colouring gap are exactly
$$\boxed{K_n\quad\text{and}\quad K_n-e.}$$
The same theorem and equality classification hold with  $\Omega$  in place of  $SF_2$ , since those two parameters agree on every prism.

I found no substantive mathematical error or valid-input implementation error.I read the complete attached note and all three Python modules. I also ran the original complete checker, without changing its code, with assertions enabled. It exited successfully, and its generated JSON matches the attached JSON byte for byte.The one proof-scope clarification is in Corollary 4a: its reference to formula (12) establishes attainment only for  $n\ge5$ . For  $n\le4$ , add the short argument using
$$\beta_2=SF_2,\qquad
\beta_2\le\psi_{\rm sq}\le\Omega=SF_2.$$
Thus all four parameters agree in those orders, and the claimed gap is zero. This does not change the corollary.Throughout the audit below,  $n=|V(H)|$  is the base order; the prism has  $2n$  vertices.1. Deficiency, representative extraction, and exact  $\Omega$ The preliminary inequalities
$$\beta_2(G)\le\psi_{\rm sq}(G)\le\Omega(G)$$
are valid under the supplied definitions.Distinct colours on a dissociation set satisfy quorum because each coloured closed neighbourhood has size at most two. Conversely, from a sub-quorum colouring, retain one edge from each colour class containing an edge, and one vertex from each independent colour class. These retained edges form a matching. A retained singleton originally had no same-colour neighbour, so quorum permitted at most one other coloured neighbour. Restricting the coloured support preserves that degree bound, giving a feasible representative pair.The deficiency identityFor any  $X\subseteq V(H)$ , put
$$I=X\setminus N_H(X).$$
Then  $I$  is independent, and
$$N_H(I)\subseteq N_H(X)\setminus X.$$
Consequently,
$$|I|-|N_H(I)|
\ge |X\setminus N_H(X)|-|N_H(X)\setminus X|
=|X|-|N_H(X)|.$$
The reverse inequality between the two maxima follows because independent sets are particular subsets. Therefore
$$\delta(H)
=\max_{X\subseteq V(H)}\bigl(|X|-|N_H(X)|\bigr)
=n-\nu(D(H)).$$
The last equality is the Hall deficiency formula in the ordinary bipartite double cover.  $H$  may be nonbipartite;  $D(H)$  is bipartite by construction.The TP-to-PZ injectionLet  $P=V(M)$  and  $Z=V(G)\setminus(T\cup P)$ . If a TP rung has endpoints
$$t\in T,\qquad p=\tau(t)\in P,$$
and  $pq\in M$ , adjacency preservation gives
$$t\tau(q)\in E(G).$$
Here  $\tau(q)\ne p$ , because equality would imply  $q=t$ , contrary to  $T\cap P=\varnothing$ . Since  $t$  already sees the occupied vertex  $p$ , feasibility forces
$$\tau(q)\in Z.$$
Thus the rung containing  $q$  is PZ.This assignment is injective: the image rung has a unique  $P$ -endpoint  $q$ , and its unique actual mate  $p$  recovers the source rung. This remains valid when  $T$  meets both halves.Writing  $a,b,u,v$  for the numbers of TT, ZZ, TP, and PZ rungs, respectively, the counting identity is
$$|T|+|M|=n+a-b+\frac{u-v}{2}.$$
The injection gives  $u\le v$ . The TT indices form an independent set  $I$  in the quotient, and every quotient neighbour of  $I$  must be ZZ. Hence
$$|T|+|M|
\le n+|I|-|N_H(I)|
